items.title: Around the Book World: August 10, 2026
items.excerpt: A record eight Pulitzer winners and finalists disclosed AI use in their 2026 submissions, and administrator Marjorie Miller says future book entry forms will carry an AI-disclosure question. The same roundup has HarperCollins saying AI will expand audiobook voices and sound effects and drive its international translation programme.

items.title: New Guidance from COPE: An Interview with Natalie Ridgway
items.excerpt: COPE's new Code of Conduct and Core Principles deliberately contain no AI-specific clauses: Ridgway says AI tools and AI-detection tools are changing so fast that named references 'would risk being outdated by the time it was published.' Instead publishers are told to handle AI through general ethics principles and their own house policies.

items.title: One Author Published 200+ Books With AI. So?
items.excerpt: A response to the outrage over an author shipping 200+ AI-assisted titles a year, arguing that declaring a workflow impossible because it is impossible for you is just projection. Frames AI publishing volume as an operations question — pipelines and quality control — rather than a morality question.

items.title: Why Smart Authors Aren't Worried About AI
items.excerpt: Jason Hamilton makes the case that AI is not killing authorship and lays out what the writers who adapt are actually doing differently — treating the model as a production tool inside a human-run book business. Aimed at indie authors deciding whether to fight or absorb the tooling.

items.title: New BISG Head Lays Out Priorities
items.excerpt: New Book Industry Study Group executive director Allison Belan says 'AI was the first thing that came up in virtually every conversation' and is now the number one issue facing the industry. She wants BISG to move members past theory into practical AI implementation and standards work.

items.title: Literary Agents Update Ethics Rules; Seven-Figure Deal Shelved Over AI Claims
items.excerpt: Dan Holloway covers the AALA rewriting its Canon of Ethics to allow agents to work more closely with indie authors, a seven-figure deal shelved within hours of an AI allegation, and the peer-reviewed study of 14,419 self-published Amazon titles. The study finds AI-generated books are commercially viable but outsold by human-written ones.

items.title: The Published Voice: Whose Voice Are We Really Reading?
items.excerpt: Roohi Ghosh argues that once AI sits in the revision loop, 'author voice' stops being a stable idea — the line between native and non-native writing blurs and the model becomes a participant in the published text. A craft problem with direct consequences for editors, copyeditors and disclosure policy.

items.title: A Publisher Read a 95% AI Chapter — Then Asked This
items.excerpt: At a book fair a chapter that was 95% AI-written drew one question from a major imprint's buyers: how did you get it this good? Not whether it was AI — a concrete data point on how acquisition conversations are shifting from provenance to craft outcome.

items.title: Links of Interest: August 5, 2026
items.excerpt: Poets are finding their copyrighted work reproduced inside Giggle Academy's learning content, and Princeton University Press has signed with AI licensing firm Cashmere. Friedman's roundup tracks where author rights are leaking into AI products faster than contracts can cover.

items.title: A Tale of Two Seven-Figure Deals
items.excerpt: AI allegations hit two seven-figure book deals in the same week — one publisher stood by its author, the other walked away. The contrast shows there is still no shared standard for what counts as disqualifying AI use in an acquired manuscript.

items.title: The Best AI Writing Workflow: Cheap Models First, Premium Models Last
items.excerpt: After a 24-hour AI writing challenge the hosts found their default model order was backwards: run cheap models for ideation, outlining and bulk drafting, then spend premium tokens only on final prose passes. A cost-and-quality routing pattern for book-length AI workflows.

items.title: Is Opus 5 an Upgrade for Writers? — Novelcrafter Live
items.excerpt: Novelcrafter benchmarks Opus 5 against its predecessors and its Sonnet and Fable siblings on actual fiction drafting, weighing the price jump against prose quality. A practical model-selection guide for novelists running AI inside a story-bible workflow.
